# Interpreting results

*Brca1* came out of your own results table with a log2 fold change of −2.29 and
a p-value of 0.00804. Read the row straight and it says two things. The gene
falls by nearly a factor of five in basal cells between virgin and lactating
mice. A fall that big turns up by accident less than once in a hundred tries.
Is that a result?

There's a third number on the same row, and it's the one that decides.

## You ran the test 14,210 times

A [p-value]{.term def="The chance of seeing a difference at least this big
between two groups when there is no real difference at all."} answers one
narrow question about one test. It knows nothing about how many other tests you
ran, and you ran a great many of them.

The filter in Chapter 24 kept every gene reaching 1 count per million in at
least 3 of the 12 samples, which left 14,210 genes. One test per gene.

```{python}
tests = 14210
print(tests * 0.05)
```

Set your threshold at 0.05 and every gene that isn't really different still has
a one-in-twenty chance of landing under it. Take that gamble 14,210 times and
about 710 genes come back under 0.05 with nothing whatsoever going on in the
experiment.

The raw count of genes below 0.05 is close to useless on its own. Your run gave
5,390 of them in the virgin-against-lactating comparison, which is seven and a
half times the 710 that pure noise would hand you. That's more than chance
alone accounts for. It still doesn't say which of the 5,390 to believe, and
that's the question the second p-value column exists to answer.

## Two ways to pay for the tests you ran

The two corrections start in the same place. A threshold that's fine for one
test is far too generous once you've run 14,210. They part company over what
they're protecting you from.

The Bonferroni correction, named for the Italian mathematician Carlo Emilio
Bonferroni, asks what threshold makes it unlikely you have even one false
positive anywhere in the table. Divide the threshold by the number of tests.

```{python}
strongest_p = 4.47e-06
bonferroni_bar = 0.05 / 14210
print(bonferroni_bar)
print(strongest_p < bonferroni_bar)
```

The first line prints `3.5186488388458835e-06`. The `e-06` on the end means
move the decimal point six places to the left, so the bar sits at about three
and a half millionths. You'll see that notation all over a results table.

The second line is the whole argument. `4.47e-06` is the smallest p-value
anywhere in your virgin-against-lactating table. It's printed in the second
summary block below, and `by_stage["p_value"].min()` pulls it out of your own
run. Python answers `False`. The strongest gene in the whole comparison misses
the Bonferroni bar, so under that correction the comparison reports nothing.

Yoav Benjamini and Yosef Hochberg asked a different question in a 1995 paper.
Of the genes you put on your hit list, what fraction are you willing to have be
wrong? Pick that fraction, usually 0.05. Their procedure then finds the largest
p-value threshold at which the expected share of false calls among your hits
stays at or below it. That share has a name: the [false discovery rate]{.term
def="The expected fraction of the hits you report that are false positives."}.
Benjamini-Hochberg is the adjustment Chapter 24 ran, and the adjusted p-value
column in your table is what it produced.

Genomics runs on the second one. When you're testing 14,210 genes and you
expect hundreds of them to be genuinely different, a hit list where one in
twenty is wrong is a useful thing to have. An empty table isn't.

The whole analysis also runs end to end in
`scripts/ch24_differential_expression.py`, which prints one summary per
comparison. Here's the six-against-six one.

``` {.default .output}
=== basal vs luminal, 6 against 6 ===
  genes tested:                     14,210
  no variance, not testable:        0
  raw p below 0.05:                 7,279
  genes with adjusted p below 0.05: 6,199
  median p-value:                   0.0443  (near 0.5 when the test is behaving)
  strongest five by p-value:
         12293 log2FC=  -7.26 p=2.28e-13 p_adj=1.51e-09
         94088 log2FC=  +2.83 p=3.46e-13 p_adj=1.51e-09
         77220 log2FC=  -5.28 p=4.14e-13 p_adj=1.51e-09
        110308 log2FC=  -8.97 p=4.46e-13 p_adj=1.51e-09
        594844 log2FC=  -4.09 p=6.89e-13 p_adj=1.51e-09
```

And the same summary for the comparison you came in asking about.

``` {.default .output}
=== within basal only: virgin vs lactating, 2 against 2 ===
  genes tested:                     14,206
  no variance, not testable:        4
  raw p below 0.05:                 5,390
  genes with adjusted p below 0.05: 9
  median p-value:                   0.0936  (near 0.5 when the test is behaving)
  strongest five by p-value:
         56461 log2FC=  +1.35 p=4.47e-06 p_adj=2.37e-02
        109594 log2FC=  -2.01 p=4.99e-06 p_adj=2.37e-02
         68355 log2FC=  -1.16 p=5.01e-06 p_adj=2.37e-02
         14663 log2FC=  +7.26 p=7.87e-06 p_adj=2.79e-02
         67102 log2FC=  -0.93 p=1.24e-05 p_adj=3.30e-02
```

Four genes in the second run didn't vary at all inside either group, so the
test had nothing to divide by and returned no p-value for them. 14,210 minus 4
is the 14,206 on that line.

::: {.check}
In your basal-against-luminal table, 7,279 genes sit below a raw 0.05 and 6,199
below an adjusted 0.05. The adjusted count is never the larger of the two. If
the two numbers match exactly, the adjustment didn't run and you're reading the
raw column twice.
:::

Set those two blocks beside each other. Six samples a side gives 6,199 survivors
out of 7,279 raw hits. With two samples a side it's 9 out of 5,390.

::: {.trap}
Two p-value columns sit on the same row and nothing stops you reading the
wrong one. *Brca1* in the virgin-against-lactating comparison has a raw p of
0.00804 and an adjusted p of 0.0693. Quote the first and you've written a true
sentence about a number that answers a question nobody asked, in a table where
14,206 tests were run. Nothing errors.
:::

## Fold change and p-value are not two views of one number

A volcano plot puts log2 fold change on the horizontal axis and the p-value on
the vertical one, flipped so the small p-values sit at the top. A reasonable
first thought is that one of those axes is redundant. Bigger difference,
smaller p-value. Why plot both?

A p-value is not a measure of how big the difference is. It comes out of the
size of the difference divided by how much your replicates disagree with each
other. Widen the disagreement and the p-value climbs while the fold change sits
exactly where it was.

The two axes catch two different failures. A gene can move a long way on
average and still be untrustworthy, because the samples inside each group are
scattered. Another gene can move a short distance with every sample agreeing,
and the test will be confident about it. The first is a large fold change with
a poor p-value. The second is a small fold change with a good one. Each happens
constantly, and neither is a mistake.

Which is why a hit list filtered on p-value alone collects genes that barely
moved. Filter on fold change alone instead and it fills up with genes that were
measured badly.

::: {.trap}
Sort your results by fold change instead of by p-value and the top fills with
genes sitting just above the filter's floor. 1 count per million in a
20,015,386-read library is about 20 reads. A gene at 20 reads in one group and
200 in another is a tenfold change resting on 220 reads. A fold-change sort
puts it above a gene that moved 50 percent on ten thousand reads. Nothing
errors.
:::

## Walkthrough: the same gene, tested twice

You've been carrying *Brca1* since Chapter 5, and Chapter 24 tested it in both
comparisons. Here are the two rows.

| comparison | per group | log2 FC | raw p | adjusted p | rank |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| basal virgin vs basal lactating | 2 | −2.29 | 0.00804 | 0.0693 | 1,645 |
| basal vs luminal | 6 | +1.96 | 0.00265 | 0.00914 | 4,127 |

Each comparison subtracts the first group's average from the second, so the
minus sign means lower in lactating and the plus sign means higher in luminal.
A log2 fold change of −2.29 means the gene divided by 2 raised to the power
2.29. A log2 fold change of +1.96 means it multiplied by 2 raised to the power
1.96.

```{python}
print(round(2 ** 2.29, 1))
print(round(2 ** 1.96, 1))
```

The first row is a drop of 4.9-fold and the second is a rise of 3.9-fold. The
first row's adjusted p-value of 0.0693 sits above 0.05, and only 9 genes in
that whole comparison came in under the line. The second row clears it at
0.00914, as one of 6,199 that do.

Same gene, same count matrix, two comparisons. The one with the bigger fold
change is the one you can't believe.

Look at the rank column too, because it's the part that surprises people.
*Brca1* is the 1,645th strongest gene in the comparison that fails and the
4,127th strongest in the comparison that passes. A rank tells you about the
company a gene is keeping, and nothing at all about whether you can believe it.

What changed between the two rows is the number of mice.

### Why two replicates a side isn't enough

Two numbers per group is everything the test has. The gap between those two
numbers is the only estimate of biological variation available to it, and two
mice that happen to land close together look exactly like precision. A t-test
has no way to tell that apart from a gene that's genuinely stable.

There's a diagnostic for this, and it's one number. Look at the median p-value
across every gene you tested.

If nothing at all differed between the groups, and the test were handing back
honest p-values, those p-values would spread evenly between 0 and 1. Half above
0.5, half below. The median would land near 0.5.

Yours is 0.0936.

A median that low means one of two things. Either a great many genes really are
different, or the test isn't giving you honest p-values. The number can't
separate those two on its own. Benjamini-Hochberg answers the practical half:
of the 5,390 genes under a raw 0.05, nine survive. Whatever crushed the
distribution, it isn't several thousand genes you could name.

Now compare the six-against-six run. Its median is lower still, 0.0443, and
6,199 genes survive correction. That's what widespread real differences look
like. Basal and luminal cells are two different kinds of cell, and the whole
transcriptome says so. Two mice against two mice crushes the distribution just
as hard and leaves you nine genes.

### What a working analyst would have run

The test behind those tables is a t-test on log counts per million. It's there
because you can read every line that produces it, and you met all of those
lines by Chapter 21.

It isn't what somebody who does this for a living would run. Count data breaks
it in two places. Counts aren't normally distributed, and a t-test assumes they
are. And a gene measured at 20 reads is proportionally noisier than the same
gene measured at 2,000, in a way a t-test has no parameter for.

The tools built for this are DESeq2 and edgeR. Both fit a negative binomial
model, which is a distribution for counts that vary more than pure counting
noise would predict. Each one also borrows information across genes to pin down
that extra variation. Neither is written in Python, and this book doesn't teach
R. The derivations live in the papers behind them, and you now know what to
search for.

*Brca1* is exactly the kind of gene where that bites. Across the 12 samples its
raw count runs from 17 to 494, in libraries holding between 20,015,386 and
24,723,827 reads each. Both basal lactating samples sit at the bottom of that
range, at 20 reads and 17. The log2 fold change of −2.29 rests on those two.

::: {.why}
An RNA-seq methods section names its test in a line or two, and the two names
you'll meet most often are DESeq2 and edgeR. That line tells you what the model
assumed about the data, and which correction produced the adjusted column. Your
Chapter 24 table carries the same column headings out of a test that assumed
something different. Telling those two apart is most of what reading a methods
section is.
:::

## Gene sets, and how to over-read one

The 6,199 Entrez IDs that survived correction aren't something a person can
read. There's a standard next move for a list that size, and it's called gene
set enrichment. Take a collection of pre-defined gene groups, each one a
process somebody curated. Then ask which of those groups turn up in your hit
list more often than chance would put them there. It's a counting question.
Free web pages will run it on a pasted list of IDs, and this book doesn't walk
you through one.

Enrichment is also the easiest place in this pipeline to fool yourself, for two
reasons that have nothing to do with the software.

Your hit list depends on the threshold you picked. Move the threshold and the
enrichment answer moves with it, and nothing in the output records which
threshold produced it.

The gene sets themselves overlap heavily. One real biological effect comes back
as a dozen related categories, each carrying its own p-value. A dozen p-values
about a single effect reads on the page like a dozen findings.

Report it as what it is: a description of the hit list you already had, rather
than fresh evidence for it.

## If it breaks

::: {.ifbreaks}
::: {.errfix err="KeyError: 12189"}
Python is talking, and it's saying 12189 isn't in the index of the table you
asked. *Brca1* clears the count filter, so the usual cause is an index holding
Entrez IDs as text rather than as numbers. `table.loc["12189"]` and
`table.loc[12189]` are two different requests. Print `table.index[:5]` and look
for quote marks.
:::

::: {.errfix err="Whole runs of rows share one identical adjusted p-value"}
Nothing is wrong. An adjusted p-value is never allowed to fall as the raw
p-value rises. The step that enforces that is a running minimum, taken from the
bottom of the sorted list upward, and it flattens neighboring values onto one
number. That's why the five strongest genes in your basal-against-luminal table
all carry an adjusted p of 1.51e-09. Sort on the raw column when you want the
order back.
:::

::: {.errfix err="Your adjusted p-values came out smaller than your raw ones"}
The adjustment can push a p-value up or leave it alone, and it can't do
anything else. If yours went down, you divided where you should have
multiplied. The formula is the raw p-value times the number of tests, divided
by that gene's rank in the sorted list, capped at 1.
:::
:::
